title: Duties of the Heart
hookLine: Bahya ibn Paquda teaches that outward practice needs inner work

lines: A LIST OF THINGS TO CHECK OFF.
WHAT DOESN'T FIT IN A BOX.
cards: A to-do list on the fridge: groceries, call the dentist, return the library book. By evening, every item is checked off.

But nothing on it says be patient with the kids, or stop resenting your brother, or trust that tomorrow will hold. Those don't fit in a box. Yesterday's king had the right intentions and the wrong actions.
Today's teacher saw the opposite risk: you can do every right action and leave the heart behind. His name was Bahya ibn Paquda, a judge in Muslim Spain, and his book is called Duties of the Heart.

teach.b: Bahya divides the commandments into two kinds. Duties of the limbs, things you do with your body: keep the Sabbath, give charity, pray aloud, eat this and not that.
And duties of the heart, things that happen inside: believing God is one, trusting God, loving God, being humble, being sorry for wrong, examining yourself honestly.
In his introduction he says he found long, careful books on the outward duties and very little on the inner ones, so he wrote this one to fill the gap. One proof text comes from the Shema.

In the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: "And thou shalt love the LORD thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy might." Love can't be done with your hands; it's a duty of the heart.

teach.h: THE LORD LOOKETH ON THE HEART.
teach.b: The same idea sounds in the story of David's anointing, where the prophet is told: "man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart."
Bahya arranges the book in gates, one for each inner duty, including a whole gate on trust. He isn't against outward practice; the limbs and the heart need each other.

In a picture: commandments with no heart are like a lamp with no oil, and good intentions with no deeds are just as incomplete. In one story, a pious man meets soldiers coming home from battle with their spoils.

teach.h: THE LESSER WAR AND THE GREATER WAR.
teach.b: He tells them they've come back from the lesser war, and must now prepare for the greater one, inside: the struggle with your own inclinations. No army can fight that one for you.

how: Duties of the Heart is studied in Jewish ethical and spiritual learning, especially in the Musar tradition, and its gate on trust in God is read on its own by some as a guide to bitachon.

o: a judge who wrote of commandments kept in the heart
a king told his actions didn't please God
a soldier home from the lesser war with spoils

games.q: duties of the heart — tap the pairs.
p: things you do with your body
the battle the soldiers came home from

s: Bahya taught that outward practice doesn't matter
he says the limbs and the heart need each other; neither is complete alone.
Bahya wrote the book because he saw little written about the inner duties
in his introduction he says the outward duties had long books, and the inner ones very little.
the greater war in Bahya's story is a battle with a foreign army
the pious man tells the soldiers the greater war is the struggle with their own inclinations.

games.q: you are the pious man. soldiers come home from battle, proud, carrying spoils. what do you say to them?
o: congratulate them; the hard part is over.
tell them the greater war is still ahead, inside.
games.why: he tells them they have returned from the lesser war, and must prepare for the greater one: the struggle with their own inclinations.

practice: Choose one thing from Bahya's list that nobody can see you do: hand one worry over for these breaths, be glad of someone who did better than you, or look honestly at one moment from yesterday.
Notice how it feels to leave no mark on any list. If you pray, you can bring it into your prayer in your own words.

wordCard.voice: Bahya. A judge in Muslim Spain who wrote Duties of the Heart, teaching that trust, love and humility are commandments too, done inside the heart. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: 'duties of the hearts', the title of Bahya's book.

carryVoice: Your line: the greater war is inside. Some duties never fit on a list. That's day nine hundred twenty-five.
